passages.text: PHLOGISTON, in chemistry, the principle of inflammability, or that substance which, being contained in bodies, renders them capable of burning.
When a body burns, the phlogiston escapes from it, and what remains is the body deprived of its inflammable principle; thus metals, when calcined, are reduced to a calx or earth.
Charcoal, being very rich in phlogiston, restores it to a calx when they are heated together, and the metal is revived.
Air is necessary to burning, because it receives the phlogiston as it is set free; a candle in a close vessel goes out when the air is saturated with it.

It is remarkable that metals gain weight by calcination, though they are said to lose something; which some explain by supposing phlogiston to be lighter than nothing, or to possess a principle of levity.
The doctrine was established by Stahl, from the earlier opinions of Becher, and is now received by almost all chemists.

The phlogiston theory, now obsolete, held that a fire-like element called phlogiston is contained within combustible bodies and released during combustion. It was first stated in 1667 by Johann Joachim Becher and put together more formally by Georg Ernst Stahl.
In the theory, burning a metal released phlogiston and left its calx; heating the calx with charcoal, which was thought rich in phlogiston, turned it back into metal.
Air was thought to absorb phlogiston, and burning stopped in a closed space once the air was saturated.
Metals were found to gain mass when burned. Some supporters suggested that phlogiston had negative weight.
Antoine Lavoisier showed in the 1770s and 1780s that combustion is a reaction with oxygen, and the theory was abandoned by the end of the 18th century.
A calx is now known as an oxide: the metal combined with oxygen. Charcoal turns it back into metal by removing the oxygen.

reasons: Same headword: PHLOGISTON and Phlogiston theory.
Rare terms appear in both: calx, Stahl, Becher, negative weight.
Combustion scores lower because it describes the modern view, not the old theory.

alignments.label: What burning is

britannica.quote: When a body burns, the phlogiston escapes from it

wikipedia.quote: combustion is a reaction with oxygen

alignments.note: Reversed: burning does not release something, it takes up oxygen.

alignments.label: Calx

britannica.quote: metals, when calcined, are reduced to a calx

wikipedia.quote: A calx is now known as an oxide

alignments.note: The observation holds. The calx is the metal plus oxygen, not the metal minus phlogiston.

alignments.label: Charcoal revives metal

britannica.quote: restores it to a calx when they are heated together, and the metal is revived

wikipedia.quote: Charcoal turns it back into metal by removing the oxygen

alignments.note: Right result, reversed reason: charcoal takes oxygen away rather than giving phlogiston back.

alignments.label: Candle in a closed vessel

britannica.quote: a candle in a close vessel goes out

wikipedia.quote: burning stopped in a closed space

alignments.note: The observation is sound. Today the candle goes out because the oxygen is used up.

alignments.label: Lighter than nothing

britannica.quote: supposing phlogiston to be lighter than nothing

wikipedia.quote: Some supporters suggested that phlogiston had negative weight

alignments.note: Both report the same rescue of the theory. The weight gain was the clue that led to oxygen.

britannica.quote: established by Stahl, from the earlier opinions of Becher

wikipedia.quote: first stated in 1667 by Johann Joachim Becher and put together more formally by Georg Ernst Stahl

alignments.label: Accepted by all

britannica.quote: is now received by almost all chemists

wikipedia.quote: the theory was abandoned by the end of the 18th century

alignments.note: True in 1778, no longer: within twenty years almost no chemist held it.

suggestedQuestions: Why did metals gain weight when burned, according to the 1778 entry?

Why did metals gain weight when burned,.answer: The entry calls it remarkable and reports that some explained it by supposing phlogiston to be lighter than nothing [B5]. Wikipedia records the same idea of negative weight [W4]. The real reason is that the metal combines with oxygen from the air, which adds weight [W6].

What replaced the phlogiston theory?.answer: Lavoisier's oxygen theory. Wikipedia says he showed that combustion is a reaction with oxygen, and that phlogiston was abandoned by the end of the 18th century [W5]. In 1778 the entry still says almost all chemists accept phlogiston [B6].
